article.title: Is a Trump-Biden rematch inevitable?
article.subtitle: No, but I can't for the life of me figure out what prediction markets are thinking

extraction.summary: Silver argues that prediction markets (via ElectionBettingOdds.com) underprice a 2024 Biden-Trump rematch. They give each candidate about 65-67% to be nominated, which implies a 44% rematch probability if the two events are independent. He builds his own estimates by decomposing each nomination into scenario risks: actuarial and health risk, a late-entering challenger, voluntary withdrawal, legal jeopardy, and a 'typical' primary loss. That gets him to 80-85% for Biden and about 75% for Trump. He supports this with an old FiveThirtyEight empirical curve linking early national primary polling to nomination odds: 50%+ maps to 90%+. He also checks the internal consistency of market prices, using the conditional general-election odds they imply. The article is not paywall-truncated, though it was the first paid post. Model content is modest: it is mostly a judgmental scenario-decomposition exercise and a critique of prediction markets.
models_discussed: prediction markets (ElectionBettingOdds.com aggregating Betfair, Smarkets, PredictIt, Polymarket)
FiveThirtyEight (Silver era) early-primary-polling vs nomination-probability analysis

findings.statement: To derive the market-implied probability of a joint outcome (a Biden-Trump rematch), Silver multiplies the two separate nomination probabilities, assuming the events are independent: 65% x 67% = 44%.

quantities.name: Biden market nomination probability
quantities.context: ElectionBettingOdds.com, Sept 18 2023 (chart); rounded to 65% in text

findings.rationale: In a footnote he says he can't think of a good first-order reason to think the events are correlated.
findings.evidence_quote: Assuming that Biden and Trump’s odds are independent from one another, that means the chance of a rematch is only 65% x 67% = 44%.
findings.europe_note: Joint events such as two party leaders both surviving to an election can be combined this way, but correlation should be checked before multiplying.

findings.statement: A vintage FiveThirtyEight (Silver-era) analysis shows a sigmoid relationship between a candidate's early national primary polling average (January-June of the year before the election) and the chance of winning the nomination. A candidate at 50% or higher has a 90%+ chance. Reading the chart, about 15% maps to roughly 10%, about 30% to roughly 45%, about 40% to roughly 75%, and 60% to roughly 97%.
findings.rationale: Uses historical data on how early primary leaders fared.
findings.evidence_quote: a candidate polling at 50 percent or higher in national primary polls is empirically in a very strong position, equating to a 90 percent or higher chance of being his party’s nominee.
findings.europe_note: A similar logistic mapping from early polls to final outcome could be fitted for party leadership contests or for party-placing probabilities.

findings.statement: Silver says the FiveThirtyEight early-polling curve understates a leader's chances later in the cycle. It was built on January-June polling of the pre-election year, and polling later in the year (with the leader still strong) should be more predictive.
findings.rationale: Polls gain predictive power as the calendar advances.
findings.evidence_quote: It pertains to polling conducted in the first half of the year before the election (that is, January-June). We’re now in the second half of the year, and Trump’s polling has only gotten stronger.
findings.europe_note: Any poll-to-outcome mapping should condition on time remaining before the vote.

findings.statement: Silver estimates nomination probabilities by summing the probabilities of distinct failure scenarios. For Trump: about 10% for losing in 'typical' fashion (for example, caught from behind in Iowa), 5% for a health issue, and 10% for legal jeopardy forcing withdrawal or a voter turn. That totals roughly 25%, so Trump has about a 75% nomination chance.
findings.rationale: Decomposing risk into scenarios makes market prices easier to judge.
findings.evidence_quote: That gets me to about a 75 percent chance of his being nominated again.
findings.europe_note: Leader-replacement risk before European elections can be modeled with the same scenario decomposition.

findings.statement: For Biden, Silver decomposes non-nomination risk as follows: roughly 10% for death or a significant medical event forcing withdrawal, a smaller chance of voluntary withdrawal (LBJ-style), and an even smaller chance that a new entrant defeats him. That totals 15-20%, so Biden has an 80-85% nomination chance.
findings.evidence_quote: That’s how I get to a 15 or 20 percent chance of someone other than Biden being the nominee.

findings.statement: For candidate health risk, Silver starts from an actuarial base rate: about 5% one-year mortality for an average 80-year-old non-Hispanic white man. He adjusts it down for Biden's better-than-average health and medical care, and shortens the horizon because the convention is 11 months away. He then adds non-fatal disabling events such as strokes, arriving at about 10% combined.
findings.rationale: Non-fatal events like strokes would also likely end a campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: The chance of an average non-Hispanic white man of Biden’s age (80) dying in the next year are about 5 percent.

findings.statement: Silver sets Trump's health-related exit risk (5%) below Biden's (10%). The reasons are partly age (77 vs 80, despite Trump being overweight) and partly that Trump would be more stubborn and Republican voters more forgiving of a health issue.
findings.rationale: Probability of exit depends on behavioral response to a health event, not just on mortality.
findings.evidence_quote: I think Trump would be more stubborn in the event of a health-related complication than Biden would be

findings.statement: Silver argues prediction markets on American elections contain a lot of 'dumb money' compared with other events they forecast. He thinks bettors overweight media chatter, for example about Biden withdrawing, and neglect structural facts such as how late it is for new entrants.
findings.rationale: Market prices reflect media narratives rather than base rates.
findings.evidence_quote: I suspect bettors at prediction markets are overweighting media chatter about Biden
findings.europe_note: Treat betting markets as a noisy benchmark, not ground truth.

findings.statement: Silver checks market prices for internal consistency. If markets were pricing large legal risk to Trump's nomination, that risk should also lower his general-election odds, both because a conviction is more likely by November and because swing voters care more. Instead, markets imply a 45% general-election win chance conditional on nomination (29.6/66.8), which Silver calls high for a challenger facing an incumbent.
findings.rationale: Coherence between linked markets reveals whether a risk is actually priced.
findings.evidence_quote: these markets imply a 45 percent chance of Trump winning the general election conditional upon being nominated, which is pretty high for someone running against an incumbent.
findings.europe_note: Cross-check related market or forecast quantities, such as party vote share and leader survival, for coherence.

findings.statement: In this case, the play-money Manifold markets gave Trump 75% and Biden 83% for their nominations, nearly matching Silver's estimates. Silver suggests the play-money market seemed more accurate than real-money sites like PredictIt.
findings.evidence_quote: the play-money market seems to be more accurate than real-money sites like PredictIt.

findings.statement: Silver warns that a market can be stale or mis-specified. A market he cited giving about a 10% chance of Trump being jailed by 2028 turned out to be an inactive 2021 market. A newer market gave about 50% by 2030, and he notes its long time frame limits usefulness.
findings.evidence_quote: the market I linked to before is from 2021 and is no longer active.

findings.statement: FiveThirtyEight (2023) dropped Marianne Williamson from its Democratic primary polling averages, so Silver used RCP's average instead. Per the RCP chart, the average was Biden 66.7, Kennedy 11.9, and Williamson 5.6.
findings.evidence_quote: FiveThirtyEight actually dropped Williamson from their polling averages, so here are the RCP numbers instead
findings.europe_note: Decisions about which minor candidates or parties to include in averages affect usability.

findings.statement: The FiveThirtyEight 2024 Republican primary national average shown in the article adjusts each poll for recency, sample size, methodology and house effects. It displays a band in which 95% of polls are projected to fall. As of Sept 15, 2023 the average was Trump 55.5, DeSantis 14.2, Ramaswamy 7.6, Haley 6.1 and Pence 4.7.

quantities.name: poll range band
quantities.context: of polls projected to fall in range

findings.europe_note: The same four poll adjustments (recency, sample size, methodology, house effects) and the poll-range band apply to multiparty averages.

findings.statement: In multi-candidate primaries, a front-runner's opponents gain ground in head-to-head matchup polls; the amount depends on the poll. Races should therefore tighten when the field narrows to two or three candidates.
findings.evidence_quote: Trump’s opponents do gain some ground in head-to-head matchups
findings.europe_note: This matters for two-round systems such as the French runoff, where the field narrows between rounds.

findings.statement: Silver says survey responses wanting 'a different candidate' should be discounted when there is no consensus alternative. In the CNN poll, two-thirds of Democrats wanted someone else, but 82% of them wanted 'just someone besides Joe Biden'; no named alternative exceeded 3%.
findings.rationale: Generic dissatisfaction doesn't translate into support for a viable challenger.
findings.evidence_quote: there is absolutely no consensus on who this “different candidate” might be
findings.europe_note: Generic leader-dissatisfaction polls overstate the real threat of a leadership challenge.

political_insights.insight: A primary challenger needs an identifiable factional coalition to be viable. Pat Buchanan had staunch conservatives in 1992; RFK Jr. lacks any Democratic faction. Even Buchanan peaked in New Hampshire, just under 40%, and lost every state.
political_insights.evidence: Buchanan never got more than 36% after New Hampshire.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: A surprising early showing by a factionless protest candidate should not move nomination odds much.

political_insights.insight: Candidates can poll decently early because of name recognition, then fade as voters learn their positions. RFK Jr. ended up viewed more favorably by Republicans than by Democrats.
political_insights.evidence: Kennedy's RCP average declined from about 20 to 11.9 between May and September 2023.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Discount early polling of well-known names whose positions clash with the party base.

political_insights.insight: Late entrants to nomination races face huge obstacles in money, staff and message. Bloomberg entered in November 2019 and flopped despite unlimited resources.
political_insights.evidence: Bloomberg's 2020 campaign won only American Samoa.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: The probability of a late-entrant victory should be low, and it falls as the calendar advances.

political_insights.insight: If an incumbent withdraws late, the vice president is the most likely replacement. In a chaotic rump process, name recognition and incumbency status matter more than electoral track record.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: In replacement scenarios, weight the designated or likely successor heavily.

political_insights.insight: Silver says LBJ's 1968 withdrawal reflected ideological vulnerability (Vietnam). Biden's weakness is concentrated on age, not ideology, because he calibrates well between party flanks.
political_insights.evidence: In the CNN poll, 49% cited age as their biggest concern about Biden.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Concerns limited to age do not create an opening for an ideological challenger.

political_insights.insight: Republican primary voters had not shown concern about Trump's indictments, but swing voters might care about a conviction even if partisans don't.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Model scandal effects differently for primary electorates and general electorates.

political_insights.insight: Parties have a long history of not renominating losing candidates. Trump is an exception because most Republicans believe the 2020 election was stolen.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Historical base rates can fail when the electorate rejects the premise behind them.

political_insights.insight: A 45% general-election win chance for a challenger against an incumbent is, in Silver's view, pretty high.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: This implies an incumbency prior favoring the incumbent.

references.description: Vintage FiveThirtyEight post on chance of winning nomination based on early polling average

open_questions: What is the exact functional form and dataset behind the FiveThirtyEight early-polling-to-nomination curve?
How does the relationship between primary polls and nomination odds evolve from the second half of the pre-election year to the primaries?
How should correlation between the two nominations be treated when computing joint probabilities?
